[[File:Steiner-erz-def-s.svg|thumb|1. Definition of the Steiner generation of a conic section]]
The '''Steiner conic''' or more precisely '''Steiner's generation of a conic''', named after the Swiss mathematician [[Jakob Steiner]], is an alternative method to define a non-degenerate [[Quadric (projective geometry)|projective conic section]] in a [[projective plane]] over a [[Field (mathematics)|field]].

The [[Quadric#Normal form of projective quadrics|usual definition]] of a conic in projective space uses a [[quadratic form]]. Another alternative definition of a conic uses a ''hyperbolic polarity''. It is due to ''[[Karl Georg Christian von Staudt|K. G. C. von Staudt]]'' and sometimes called a [[von Staudt conic]]. The disadvantage of von Staudt's definition is that it only works when the underlying field has odd [[characteristic (field)|characteristic]].

== Definition of a Steiner conic ==
*Given two [[Pencil (mathematics)|pencils]] <math>B(U),B(V)</math> of lines at two points <math>U,V</math> (all lines containing <math>U</math> and  <math>V</math> resp.) and a projective but not perspective mapping <math>\pi</math> of <math>B(U)</math> onto <math>B(V)</math>. Then the intersection points of corresponding lines form a non-degenerate projective conic section<ref>{{harvnb|Coxeter|1993}}, p.&nbsp;80</ref><ref name=Hartmann1>{{harvnb|Hartmann|loc=p. 38}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Merserve|1983|loc=p. 65}}</ref><ref>''Jacob Steiner's Vorlesungen über synthetische Geometrie'', B. G. Teubner, Leipzig 1867 (from Google Books: [https://books.google.com/books?id=jCgPAAAAQAAJ (German) Part II follows Part I]) Part II, pg. 96</ref> (figure 1)
[[File:Persp-geradenb-s.svg|thumb|2. Perspective mapping between lines]]
A ''perspective'' mapping <math>\pi</math> of a pencil <math>B(U)</math> onto a pencil <math>B(V)</math> is a [[bijection]] (1-1 correspondence) such that corresponding lines intersect on a fixed line <math>a</math>, which is called the ''axis'' of the perspectivity <math>\pi</math> (figure 2).

A ''projective'' mapping is a finite product of perspective mappings.

''Simple example:'' If one shifts in the first diagram point <math>U</math> and its pencil of lines onto <math>V</math> and rotates the shifted pencil around <math>V</math> by a fixed angle <math>\varphi</math> then the shift (translation) and the rotation generate  a projective mapping <math>\pi</math> of the pencil at point <math>U</math> onto the pencil at <math>V</math>. From the [[inscribed angle theorem]] one gets: The intersection points of corresponding lines form a circle.

Examples of commonly used fields are the real numbers <math>\R</math>, the rational numbers <math>\Q</math> or the complex numbers <math>\C</math>. The construction also works over finite fields, providing examples in finite [[projective plane]]s.

''Remark:''
The fundamental theorem for projective planes states,<ref name=Hartmann2>{{harvnb|Hartmann|loc=p. 19}}</ref> that a projective mapping in a projective plane over a field ([[pappian plane]]) is uniquely determined by prescribing the images of three lines. That means that, for the Steiner generation of a conic section, besides two points <math>U,V</math> only the images of 3 lines have to be given. These 5 items (2 points, 3 lines) uniquely determine the conic section.

''Remark:''
The notation "perspective" is due to the dual statement: The projection of the points on a line <math>a</math> from a center <math>Z</math> onto a line <math>b</math> is called a [[perspectivity]] (see [[#Steiner generation of a dual conic|below]]).<ref name=Hartmann2 />
[[File:Steiner-erz-beisp-s.svg|thumb|3. Example of a Steiner generation: generation of a point]]

== Example ==
For the following example the images of the lines <math> a,u,w</math> (see picture) are given: <math>\pi(a)=b, \pi(u)=w, \pi(w)=v</math>. The projective mapping <math>\pi</math> is the product of the following perspective mappings <math>\pi_b,\pi_a</math>: 1) <math>\pi_b</math> is the perspective mapping of the pencil at point <math>U</math> onto the pencil at point <math>O</math> with axis <math>b</math>. 2) <math>\pi_a</math> is the perspective mapping of the pencil at point <math>O</math> onto the pencil at point <math>V</math> with axis <math>a</math>.
First one should check that <math>\pi=\pi_a\pi_b</math> has the properties: <math>\pi(a)=b, \pi(u)=w, \pi(w)=v</math>. Hence for any line <math>g</math> the image <math>\pi(g)=\pi_a\pi_b(g)</math> can be constructed and therefore the images of an arbitrary set of points. The lines <math>u</math> and <math>v</math> contain only the conic points <math>U</math> and <math>V</math> resp.. Hence <math>u</math> and <math>v</math> are tangent lines of the generated conic section.

A ''proof'' that this method generates a conic section follows from switching to the affine restriction with line <math>w</math> as the [[line at infinity]], point <math>O</math> as the origin of a coordinate system with points <math>U,V</math> as [[point at infinity|points at infinity]] of the ''x''- and ''y''-axis resp. and point <math>E=(1,1)</math>. The affine part of the generated curve appears to be the [[hyperbola]] <math>y=1/x</math>.<ref name=Hartmann1 />

''Remark:''
#The Steiner generation of a conic section provides simple methods for the construction of [[ellipse]]s, [[parabola]]s and [[hyperbola]]s which are commonly called the ''parallelogram methods''.
#The figure that appears while constructing a point (figure 3) is the 4-point-degeneration of [[Pascal's theorem]].<ref>{{harvnb|Hartmann|loc=p. 32}}</ref>

== Steiner generation of a dual conic ==
[[File:Ellipse-dual-s.svg|thumb|dual ellipse]]
[[File:Steiner-conic-dual-def-s.svg|thumb|Steiner generation of a dual conic]]
[[File:Perspektive-abbildung-def-s.svg|thumb|definition of a perspective mapping]]

=== Definitions and the dual generation ===
Dualizing (see [[duality (projective geometry)]]) a projective plane means exchanging the ''points'' with the ''lines'' and the operations ''intersection'' and ''connecting''. The dual structure of a projective plane is also a projective plane. The dual plane of a pappian plane is pappian and can also be coordinatized by homogeneous coordinates. A nondegenerate ''dual conic'' section is analogously defined by a quadratic form.

A dual conic can be generated by Steiner's dual method:

*Given the point sets of two lines <math>u,v</math> and a projective but not perspective mapping <math>\pi</math> of <math>u</math> onto <math>v</math>. Then the lines connecting corresponding points form a dual non-degenerate projective conic section.

A ''perspective mapping'' <math>\pi</math> of the point set of a line <math>u</math> onto the point set of a line <math>v</math> is a [[bijection]] (1-1 correspondence) such that the connecting lines of corresponding points intersect at a fixed point <math>Z</math>, which is called the ''centre'' of the perspectivity <math>\pi</math> (see figure).

A ''projective '' mapping is a finite sequence of perspective mappings.

It is usual, when dealing with dual and common conic sections, to call the common conic section a ''point conic'' and the dual conic a ''line conic''.

In the case that the underlying field has <math>\operatorname{Char} =2</math> all the tangents of a point conic intersect in a point, called the ''knot'' (or ''nucleus'') of the conic. Thus, the dual of a non-degenerate point conic is a subset of points of a dual line and not an oval curve (in the dual plane). So, only in the case that <math>\operatorname{Char}\ne2</math> is the dual of a non-degenerate point conic a non-degenerate line conic.

=== Examples ===
[[File:Steiner-conic-dual-ex2.svg|thumb|upright=1.2|Dual Steiner conic defined by two perspectivities <math>\pi_A, \pi_B</math>]]
[[File:Steiner-dual-example-s.svg|300px|thumb|example of a Steiner generation of a dual conic]]
'''(1) Projectivity given by two perspectivities:'''<br>
Two lines <math>u,v</math> with intersection point <math>W</math> are given and a projectivity <math>\pi</math> from <math>u</math> onto <math>v</math> by two perspectivities <math>\pi_A,\pi_B</math>  with centers <math>A,B</math>. <math>\pi_A</math> maps line <math>u</math> onto a third line <math>o</math>, <math>\pi_B</math> maps line <math>o</math> onto line <math>v</math> (see diagram). Point <math>W</math> must not lie on the lines <math>\overline{AB},o</math>. Projectivity <math>\pi</math> is the composition of the two perspectivities:  <math> \ \pi=\pi_B\pi_A</math>. Hence a point <math>X</math> is mapped onto <math>\pi(X)=\pi_B\pi_A(X)</math> and the line <math>x=\overline{X\pi(X)}</math> is an element of the dual conic defined by <math>\pi</math>.<br>
(If <math>W</math> would be a fixpoint, <math>\pi</math> would be perspective.<ref>H. Lenz: ''Vorlesungen über projektive Geometrie'', BI, Mannheim, 1965, S. 49.</ref>)

'''(2) Three points and their images are given:'''<br>
The following example is the dual one given above for a Steiner conic.<br> 
The images of the points <math> A,U,W</math> are given: <math>\pi(A)=B, \, \pi(U)=W,\,  \pi(W)=V</math>. The projective mapping <math>\pi</math> can be represented by the product of the following perspectivities <math>\pi_B,\pi_A</math>: 
# <math>\pi_B</math> is the perspectivity of the point set of line <math>u</math> onto the point set of line <math>o</math> with centre <math>B</math>. 
# <math>\pi_A</math> is the perspectivity of the point set of line <math>o</math> onto the point set of line <math>v</math> with centre <math>A</math>.
One easily checks that the projective mapping <math>\pi=\pi_A\pi_B</math> fulfills <math>\pi(A)=B,\, \pi(U)=W, \, \pi(W)=V </math>. Hence for any arbitrary point <math>G</math> the image <math>\pi(G)=\pi_A\pi_B(G)</math> can be constructed and line <math>\overline{G\pi(G)}</math> is an element of a non degenerate dual conic section.  Because the points <math>U</math> and <math>V</math> are contained in the lines <math>u</math>, <math>v</math> resp.,the points <math>U</math> and <math>V</math> are points of the conic and the lines <math>u,v</math> are tangents at <math>U,V</math>.

{{clear}}

== Intrinsic conics in a linear incidence geometry ==
The Steiner construction defines the conics in a planar linear incidence geometry (two points determine at most one line and two lines intersect in at most one point) ''intrinsically'', that is, using only the collineation group. Specifically, <math>E(T,P)</math> is the ''conic at point'' <math>P</math> ''afforded by the collineation'' <math>T</math>, consisting of the intersections of <math>L</math> and <math>T(L)</math> for all lines <math>L</math> through <math>P</math>. If <math>T(P)=P</math> or  <math>T(L)=L</math> for some <math>L</math> then the conic is ''degenerate''. For example, in the real coordinate plane, the affine type (ellipse, parabola, hyperbola) of <math>E(T,P)</math> is determined by the trace and determinant of the matrix component of <math>T</math>, independent of <math>P</math>.

By contrast, the collineation group of the real hyperbolic plane <math>\mathbb{H}^2</math>consists of isometries. Consequently, the intrinsic conics comprise a small but varied subset of the ''general'' conics, curves obtained from the intersections of projective conics with a hyperbolic domain. Further, unlike the Euclidean plane, there is no overlap between the ''direct'' <math>E(T,P);</math> <math>T</math> preserves orientation – and the ''opposite'' <math>E(T,P);</math> <math>T</math> reverses orientation. The direct case includes ''central'' (two perpendicular lines of symmetry) and non-central conics, whereas every opposite conic is central. Even though direct and opposite central conics cannot be congruent, they are related by a quasi-symmetry defined in terms of complementary angles of parallelism. Thus, in any inversive model of <math>\mathbb{H}^2</math>, each direct central conic is birationally equivalent to an opposite central conic.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sarli |first=John |date=April 2012 |title=Conics in the hyperbolic plane intrinsic to the collineation group |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/s00022-012-0115-5 |journal=Journal of Geometry |language=en |volume=103 |issue=1 |pages=131–148 |doi=10.1007/s00022-012-0115-5 |s2cid=119588289 |issn=0047-2468|url-access=subscription }}</ref> In fact, the central conics represent all genus 1 curves with real shape invariant <math>j\geq1</math>. A minimal set of representatives is obtained from the central direct conics with common center and axis of symmetry, whereby the shape invariant is a function of the ''eccentricity'', defined in terms of the distance between <math>P</math> and <math>T(P)</math>. The [[Orthogonal trajectory|orthogonal trajectories]] of these curves represent all genus 1 curves with <math>j\leq1</math>, which manifest as either irreducible cubics or bi-circular quartics. Using the elliptic curve addition law on each trajectory, every general central conic in <math>\mathbb{H}^2</math>decomposes uniquely as the sum of two intrinsic conics by adding pairs of points where the conics intersect each trajectory.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sarli |first=John |date=2021-10-22 |title=The Elliptic Curve Decomposition of Central Conics in the Real Hyperbolic Plane |url=https://www.researchsquare.com/article/rs-936116/v1 |doi=10.21203/rs.3.rs-936116/v1|type=Preprint}}</ref>
